title: Surface Tension and Surface Energy
short_intro: Surface tension is the property of a liquid surface by virtue of which it tends to minimize its surface area, arising from intermolecular cohesive forces. It is quantitatively measured as the force acting normally per unit length on an imaginary line drawn on the liquid surface.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of surface tension, molecular theory of surface tension, surface energy, excess pressure inside liquid drops and soap bubbles, capillarity, and angle of contact.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Work done in blowing bubbles, coalescence of drops, capillary rise accounting for meniscus, temperature and impurity effects on surface tension, and rigorous mathematical formulations of excess pressure.

concept_notes.heading: Molecular Theory of Surface Tension
bullets: Molecules deep inside the liquid experience balanced cohesive forces from surrounding molecules within a sphere of molecular activity.
Molecules within a surface layer of thickness equal to the range of molecular force (approx 10<sup>-9</sup> m) experience a net inward attractive force.
Bringing a molecule from the interior to the surface requires work against this inward force, which is stored as potential energy at the surface.

concept_notes.heading: Surface Energy and Surface Tension
bullets: Surface energy is defined as the potential energy per unit surface area of the liquid film.
Surface tension (T) is numerically equal to the surface energy per unit area under isothermal conditions.
Dimension of surface tension is [MT<sup>-2</sup>] and its SI unit is N/m or J/m<sup>2</sup>.

concept_notes.heading: Excess Pressure across Curved Surfaces
bullets: Due to surface tension, molecules on a curved liquid surface experience a net inward force, creating an excess pressure on the concave side.
For a spherical liquid drop of radius R, the excess pressure is given by P = 2T/R.
For a soap bubble in air, which has two free surfaces, the excess pressure is given by P = 4T/R.

concept_notes.heading: Capillarity and Angle of Contact
bullets: Angle of contact (θ) is the angle enclosed between the tangent to the liquid surface at the point of contact and the solid surface inside the liquid.
Liquids that wet the glass (e.g., water-glass) have an acute angle of contact and rise in capillaries.
Liquids that do not wet the glass (e.g., mercury-glass) have an obtuse angle of contact and are depressed in capillaries.

derivations.title: Excess Pressure Inside a Liquid Drop
derivations.conditions: Spherical drop of radius R in equilibrium
steps: Consider a spherical liquid drop of radius R and surface tension T.
Let the radius of the drop increase by a small amount ΔR due to excess pressure P inside.
Initial surface area = 4πR<sup>2</sup>, Final surface area = 4π(R + ΔR)<sup>2</sup> ≈ 4π(R<sup>2</sup> + 2RΔR).
Work done by excess pressure = Force × displacement = (P × 4πR<sup>2</sup>) × ΔR.
Equating work done to stored potential energy: P(4πR<sup>2</sup>)ΔR = T(8πRΔR).

derivations.title: Capillary Rise Formula (Jurin's Law)
derivations.conditions: Circular capillary tube of radius r dipped in a liquid of surface tension T and density ρ
steps: Let a capillary tube of radius r be dipped in a liquid of surface tension T and contact angle θ.
The liquid rises to a height h, forming a meniscus.
The upward force due to surface tension along the circumference of the meniscus is F = (2πr)T cosθ.
This upward force balances the weight of the liquid column of height h in the tube.
Weight of the liquid column W = Volume × density × g = (πr<sup>2</sup>h + V_meniscus) ρg, where V_meniscus is approximated for narrow tubes.
Equating upward force and weight: (2πr)T cosθ = πr<sup>2</sup>hρg.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Surface Tension vs Temperature Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A nearly linear downward sloping curve of Surface Tension (T) on the y-axis versus Temperature (t) on the x-axis, intersecting zero at the critical temperature.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Surface tension decreases linearly with an increase in temperature due to an increase in thermal agitation weakening intermolecular cohesive forces.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in conceptual MCQs regarding the behavior of liquids near boiling point.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Capillary Rise vs Radius Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A rectangular hyperbola representing h ∝ 1/r, showing height decreasing rapidly as tube radius increases.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: For a given liquid, narrower capillary tubes exhibit a significantly higher liquid rise compared to wider tubes.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting proportionality constants and inverse relations in numerical problems.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Jaeger's Method / Detachment of Ring Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic setup of a capillary tube or wire ring suspended from a spring balance dipping into a liquid container.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Used to experimentally determine surface tension by measuring the maximum downward force required to pull a wire ring or detach a bubble from a liquid surface.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Theoretical questions regarding experimental determination of T.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius 2 cm. Given the surface tension of soap solution is 0.03 N/m.
solution_steps: Identify given values: Radius R = 2 cm = 2 × 10<sup>-2</sup> m, Surface tension T = 0.03 N/m.
Recall the formula for excess pressure in a soap bubble: P = 4T / R.

solved_numericals.question: 8 small water drops, each of radius r, coalesce to form a single large drop of radius R. If T is the surface tension of water, find the change in surface energy.
solution_steps: Initial surface area of 8 drops: A_i = 8 × 4πr<sup>2</sup> = 32πr<sup>2</sup>.
Final surface area of large drop: A_f = 4πR<sup>2</sup> = 4π(2r)<sup>2</sup> = 16πr<sup>2</sup>.
Change in surface area: ΔA = A_f - A_i = 16πr<sup>2</sup> - 32πr<sup>2</sup> = -16πr<sup>2</sup>.

solved_numericals.question: A capillary tube of internal radius 0.5 mm is dipped vertically into water. Calculate the height to which water rises in the tube. (Surface tension of water = 0.072 N/m, angle of contact = 0°, density of water = 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>, g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>)
solution_steps: List given parameters: r = 0.5 mm = 5 × 10<sup>-4</sup> m, T = 0.072 N/m, θ = 0° (cosθ = 1), ρ = 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>, g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
Write Jurin's law formula: h = (2T cosθ) / (r ρ g).
Compute final height: h = 0.144 / 4.9 ≈ 0.02939 m = 2.94 cm.

assumptions_and_limitations: Capillary rise formulas assume a perfectly cylindrical, clean capillary tube with uniform radius throughout its length.
The meniscus is assumed to be spherical, which holds accurately only for tubes of very small radii where gravitational flattening is negligible.
Temperature is assumed to remain constant during surface energy calculations unless thermal coefficients are explicitly applied.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Surface tension is a force acting downwards into the liquid.
common_misconceptions.correct: Surface tension is a tensile force acting tangentially along the surface of the liquid.
common_misconceptions.why: Forces of cohesion inside the liquid cause an inward pull, but surface tension itself is measured as a force per unit length acting along the surface.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A soap bubble and a liquid drop of the same radius have the same excess pressure.
common_misconceptions.correct: A soap bubble has twice the excess pressure (4T/R) compared to a liquid drop (2T/R) of the same radius.
common_misconceptions.why: A soap bubble has two free surfaces (inner and outer), whereas a liquid drop has only one free surface.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Water rises above the liquid level in a capillary tube because of atmospheric pressure pushing it up.
common_misconceptions.correct: Water rises due to the inward pull of a concave meniscus creating a reduced pressure region just below it, allowing surface forces and atmospheric pressure balance to drive the column up.
common_misconceptions.why: Capillary action is fundamentally driven by adhesive and cohesive molecular interactions at the contact line.

quick_revision: Surface tension has dimensions [MT<sup>-2</sup>] and SI unit N/m.
Excess pressure is 2T/R for drops and 4T/R for soap bubbles.
Capillary rise varies inversely with tube radius (h ∝ 1/r).
Surface tension decreases linearly with increasing temperature and drops to zero at the critical temperature.
